prompts.prompt2:
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

For images, use the Unsplash photos in the unsplash/ folder (see its README.md) and import them into the media library. Don't download other images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.

finalReport:
I built the blog site, and it's running. The front page lists both posts, both posts render with all their blocks, every image loads, and a headless-browser screenshot of the front page and one post looked right.

**View it:** https://localhost:44317/ (backoffice at `/umbraco`, login admin@example.com / 1234567890). Umbraco is still running from `dotnet run`.

**What I built.** All schema, media and content was created over the MCP server; I wrote no migrations.

- **Blocks** (in the Blocks folder): Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote, and Blog Post List. The list block shows the posts under the current front page, newest first.
- **Block grids:** two 12-column grids, one for the front page and one for posts. Rich Text and Image can be full or half width.
- **Pages** (in the Pages folder):
  - **Blog Front Page:** sits under WWW and is the only type allowed there. Its content is a block grid.
  - **Blog Post:** content is a block grid. A Teaser tab holds the publish date, teaser text and teaser image that feed the front page listing.
- **Templates:** `layout`, `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost`.
- **Media:** six Unsplash photos imported into a "Blog" media folder. The photographers are credited in the hero blocks and captions.
- **Content:** the front page "Blog" has domain `/`, with a hero, the post list and a quote. The two posts are "MCP is the USB-C port for AI" and "This blog was built by an AI over MCP". Both are made entirely of blocks.
- **Code:**
  - Each block has an adapter in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` that passes a plain model to a ViewComponent.
  - The plain models are in `Models/Blocks/` and `Models/Blog/`. All markup is in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - Post lookup is in `Services/BlogPostService.cs`, registered in `ProjectComposer`.
  - Pages render blocks with `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`.
- **Styling:** I ran `npm install` and `npm run build` in the Frontend project, since `wwwroot/dist` didn't exist. `site.css` now includes the block grid column layout and rich text styles.
- **Order of work:** modeling, then content, then stop / `dotnet build` / restart, then Razor. The build had no errors or warnings, and uSync exported the new types, data types, templates, content and media.

**Things to know:**
- The first post's title is a little long for the hero, so "AI" wraps onto its own line. It looks fine, just not ideal.
- The front page and post templates use `Layout = "layout.cshtml"` in lowercase, to match the file names Umbraco created. That matters on Linux, where file names are case-sensitive.

Nothing is broken that I know of.
